turns.prompt_text: There is this handed down. Belief of this happened to me, so it's okay that I do it to you. We're kind of like the law of nature We kill because we have to eat Sometimes like with the native American situation it's entirely justified or like more spiritual in Japan. How they kind of like respect the food they're about to eat. Otherwise that are taken. However, when it's more like a powerless thing and it's like negative like it makes all of life suck and it makes you kind of existential or that dreadful feeling
turns.response_html:
That dreadful, heavy feeling comes from a very real distinction: the difference between reciprocity and gratuitous harm disguised as nature.

When cultures—like many Indigenous traditions or the Japanese practice of itadakimasu—acknowledge taking life to eat, the act is rooted in reverence, necessity, and balance. It is not an assertion of dominance; it is an admission of dependency. The life taken is honored because the taker knows they are part of a closed circle, not an apex tyrant acting out of spite. There is dignity in that relationship because it centers on gratitude rather than exploitation.

The dread creeps in when people take the harsh realities of biology and use them as a cheap moral excuse for cruelty: "I was hurt, so the world is dog-eat-dog, which means I get to hurt you."

That isn't the law of nature; that is simply unprocessed trauma wearing a philosophical mask.

  • Nature takes out of biological necessity: An animal hunts because it must survive, not to balance an emotional ledger or vindicate its own past suffering.
  • Retaliation is a human invention: Inflicting pain simply because pain was once inflicted on you is an abdication of agency. It tries to make powerlessness feel like power.

When you see people pass pain down the line while claiming "that's just how the world works," it feels suffocating because it strips life of meaning and reduces existence to an endless chain of misery. But human beings have something a food chain doesn't: the capacity for moral choice.

You don't have to accept a handed-down cycle just because someone else lacked the strength to break it. Acknowledging that the world has sharp edges doesn't require you to become another blade.

Are you watching someone in your life try to justify their behavior this way right now, or is this a weight you've been carrying from your own past?
